# Methodology {#sec-methodology}

This study evaluates coding-agent harnesses as part of a complete model--harness system. The central experimental principle is to preserve behavior that belongs to the harness while controlling external differences that would otherwise distort the comparison. Native capabilities such as delegation and provider-specific compaction therefore remain enabled where supported, whereas routing, context limits, model selection, and usage accounting are constrained when necessary to keep measurements comparable.

## Benchmark and task selection

DeepSWE v1.1 was selected as the evaluation benchmark. It contains original, long-horizon software-engineering tasks with dedicated verifiers and publishes the benchmark artifacts and evaluation trajectories required for reproducible analysis [@huang2026deepswe]. This makes it suitable for comparing autonomous coding agents without constructing and validating a new internal task set.

Running the complete benchmark across all model--harness combinations was outside the available budget. A deterministic subset of ten tasks was therefore selected from the public DeepSWE v1.1 results. For each programming language, one hard and one medium task was selected. Difficulty is derived from the solve rate of valid historical `mini-swe-agent` runs, excluding the models evaluated in this study. Hard tasks occupy the 75th--100th difficulty percentile and medium tasks the 50th--75th percentile. Within each language and difficulty stratum, the task with the highest median historical token usage is selected. This deliberately favors demanding tasks on which differences in context handling and token efficiency are more likely to become visible. The complete selection procedure is implemented in `scripts/select_deepswe_tasks.py`, and its inputs and resulting audit data are stored in `data/deepswe_task_selection_v1.1.json`.

## Model and harness selection

The harness set consists of Claude Code, OpenAI Codex CLI, Pi, and OpenCode V2. Claude Code and Codex represent first-party coding agents from major model providers. OpenCode was the second-most common first-choice harness in the internal survey described in @sec-current-state, while Pi provides a comparatively lightweight alternative. OpenCode V2 was selected instead of V1 because it is the current major redesign and is more representative of the tool's future development.

The model set spans several providers and price classes: Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Luna, Kimi K3, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, and GLM-5.3-Flash. The purpose is not to identify the strongest model in isolation, but to determine whether harness behavior remains effective across different model families.

## Experimental controls

Each trial evaluates exactly one model through one harness. Harness-native delegation remains enabled because subagent orchestration is part of the behavior under study. However, delegated calls are constrained to the same benchmark model as the parent session. This prevents a nominally single-model trial from becoming a multi-model ensemble. The Pier adapters aggregate usage across the complete parent/child session tree while retaining the root session as the main trajectory.

Provider-specific harness optimizations are otherwise retained. For example, a harness may use its native compaction or caching behavior when the selected model supports it. Equivalent features are not recreated through custom plugins in competing harnesses, because the objective is to evaluate the harnesses as practical systems rather than force their internal implementations to be identical.

A limited normalization is applied where configuration would directly distort cost comparison. GPT-5.6 Luna is restricted to a 272,000-token context window in every harness. OpenAI applies different pricing beyond this threshold [@openaiGpt56Luna]; allowing some harnesses to use the larger context while others remain below the threshold would make the measured cost depend on inconsistent context limits rather than harness efficiency. The same benchmark window is therefore enforced across all Luna runs.

Web access is disabled for benchmark agents. Each trial is evaluated only against the repository and tools supplied by the benchmark environment.

## Benchmark infrastructure

DeepSWE is executed through a fork of Pier. The fork is used because the upstream runner did not support all selected harnesses and did not expose all usage required for a fair cost comparison. The modifications are limited to experimental instrumentation and compatibility: additional harness adapters, model isolation, recursive usage accounting, and preservation of relevant cache and token fields. They do not alter the benchmark task, verifier, or repository presented to the agent.

For Claude Code and Codex, delegated-agent usage is included in the final token totals. Claude Code subagents are explicitly pinned to the benchmark model. Codex delegation remains available, but spawn-time model overrides are disabled so child agents inherit the tested model. OpenCode V2 is run through a dedicated adapter that collects root, delegated, and compaction sessions and enforces the configured model where required.

## Compatibility interventions

Compatibility changes are permitted only when they are required to make a harness communicate correctly with the intended model endpoint. Such changes are kept narrowly scoped and are not used to add capabilities to a harness.

### Codex with third-party models

Codex 0.151.0 uses the OpenAI Responses protocol, while the Fireworks-backed models are reached through a LiteLLM Chat Completions route. Direct translation through the existing gateway was not sufficient for Codex's request and reasoning semantics. A pinned CLIProxyAPI instance is therefore used as a protocol bridge:

`Codex -> Responses -> CLIProxyAPI -> Chat Completions -> LiteLLM -> Fireworks`.

The bridge performs protocol translation only. Its own retries, credential cooldowns, and model fallbacks are disabled so it cannot improve the measured harness behavior.

During the benchmark period, an upstream CLIProxyAPI defect was identified in which a streamed chunk containing both `reasoning_content` and visible `content` could produce an invalid Responses item order [@cliproxyIssue5659]. Rather than upgrade the complete bridge and introduce unrelated changes, the benchmark keeps the frozen v7.2.146 base and backports only the upstream fix [@cliproxyFix5659]. Logs from the already completed Kimi K3 run showed that the defect's triggering condition did not occur in that run, so it was retained.

### OpenCode V2 output limit

OpenCode V2.0.3 did not propagate its configured output limit into requests sent through `@ai-sdk/openai-compatible`; the upstream provider could therefore apply its own default completion limit [@opencodeIssue47398]. The benchmark configuration explicitly injects the model's output limit into the request body. This restores the intended model configuration without changing OpenCode's agent policy or tool behavior.

## Cost accounting

Cross-harness cost is calculated from recorded token and cache usage using a frozen pricing table in `benchmark/pricing.yaml`. Official model API prices are used rather than the invoice price of the underlying proxy or inference host. This separates model and harness efficiency from provider-specific discounts or surcharges.

If a trial is discarded and repeated because of a transport or gateway failure, tokens consumed by the discarded attempt remain part of the reported cost. Removing them would systematically favor configurations that fail more often. In contrast, benchmark task timeouts are treated as outcomes of the evaluated system rather than infrastructure failures and are not automatically rerun.

## Reproducibility

Benchmark components are pinned for the experiment. The primary frozen environment uses DeepSWE revision `0b9fabbb63b9104d678fe965e1632f2dd9eaa2ea`, Codex CLI 0.151.0, Claude Code 2.1.251, and Pi 0.84.4. OpenCode V2 is pinned independently to version 2.0.3. The Pier revision, compatibility-bridge image digest, model profiles, pricing table, generated configurations, and task-selection audit data are stored with the benchmark setup. Pier additionally records a `lock.json` in each result directory so that a run can be traced to the exact configuration used.
